# Chapter 2: Discrete mathematics

<!-- BEGIN HEADER (generated by tools/build.py) -->
> [Home](../../../../README.md) › [Part I — Computer Science Foundations](../../index.md) › [2. Mathematics for Computer Science](../index.md) › Chapter 2: Discrete mathematics

- **Status:** Drafted · 10 syllabus topics
<!-- END HEADER -->

Discrete mathematics is the mathematics of things that can be counted one by one: collections, pairings, arrangements and steps. It is the language of data structures, databases, algorithms and networks, and it supplies the proof techniques that show a program does what it claims.

The first lesson introduces the three structures everything else is built from: sets, relations and functions. The second counts arrangements and selections with sequences, permutations and combinations. The third covers mathematical induction, the standard way to prove a statement about every whole number, and recurrence relations, which describe the running time of recursive programs. The fourth covers two counting principles, the pigeonhole principle and inclusion-exclusion. Short Python programs, whose output is checked, make each idea concrete.

Later chapters of this subject build on this one: logic, graph theory, probability and algorithm analysis all use counting and proof by induction. Read the lessons in order.
